title: Collections: lists, tuples, dictionaries and sets

videos.script:
Until now every program you have written has held one thing at a time. One name, one number, one line of text. {{one}} Real work is never one thing. It is four thousand rows, or every file in a directory, or the words in a paragraph.

{{four}} Python gives you four containers for that, and the useful way to meet them is not as four pieces of syntax to memorise. It is as four different answers to four different questions.

{{questions}} Does the order matter? Then a list. Is it fixed, a thing that should not change after you make it? A tuple. Are you looking things up by a name rather than a position? A dictionary — and that is the one you will reach for most. Do you only care whether something is in there, and want no duplicates? A set.

{{lookup}} Here is the one that surprises people, and it is worth knowing on the first day rather than the hundredth. Asking whether something is in a list means walking the list. Asking whether it is in a set means one calculation, however big the set is. Ten items, no difference. A hundred thousand items, and the difference is a program that answers instantly against one that does not answer at all.

Lesson 20 measures that properly. Today you just need to know the question exists.

{{share}} And one more thing, which is the thing this lesson exists to prevent. A list is MUTABLE. Two names can refer to the same one, and changing it through either shows through both. That is not a flaw — it is how you pass a big thing to a function without copying it. But it is the most common surprise in the language, and there is a section here with the exact shape of the bug in it.

One record, held four different ways, and what each way makes easy.

{{record}} Here is a person: a name, a city, and three languages they speak. I will hold that four times.

{{list}} As a list — name, city, then the languages. Order is preserved, I can append a fourth language, and to find the city I have to remember it is at index one. Index one. That is the whole problem with this shape: the meaning is in my head and not in the data.

{{tuple}} As a tuple. The same thing, and now it cannot change. Which is the right choice when the record is finished — it can be a dictionary key, and nothing can quietly edit it from another function.

{{dict}} As a dictionary. Name, city, languages, each behind a key that says what it is. Now `person["city"]` reads like a sentence, order is irrelevant, and adding a field breaks nothing.

{{set}} And the languages as a set. I add Portuguese twice and it is still there once. I ask whether they speak Dutch — that is one lookup, not a walk. And I can ask what two people have in common with an ampersand, which on a list would be a loop.

{{point}} Four shapes, one record. The dictionary is the one to reach for when the fields have names, which is almost always. And the set is the one to remember the moment you write `if x in something` inside a loop.

Four questions, and they settle it every time.

{{order}} Does order matter and will it change? List. Does order matter and should it NOT change? Tuple. Is there a name for each piece? Dictionary. Do you only need membership, with no duplicates? Set.

{{lookup}} `in` on a list walks it. `in` on a set or a dictionary is one step. When that is inside a loop, it is the difference between eleven seconds and forty milliseconds — you will see exactly that in lesson 20.

{{copy}} And the one to carry out of here. Assignment does not copy. `b = a` gives the same list two names, and `list(a)` or `a.copy()` gives you a new one. If what is inside is itself a list, even that is not enough, and `deepcopy` is the answer.

{{default}} Which is also why a mutable default argument is a bug rather than a style note. It is created once, at definition, and every call that does not supply one shares it. `None` is the fix, and lesson 5 will show it again.

{{next}} Next lesson: doing something only sometimes, and doing something to everything. Conditionals, loops, and the comprehension that replaces half of them.
